```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 17_correlation_significance
title: Same correlation, different samples
questions:
  - id: same_r_different_n
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Two studies each find a correlation of $r = .30$. One has 10 pairs of
      scores and the other has 100. Using a two-tailed test with
      $\alpha = .05$, which correlation is statistically significant? Calculate
      $t$ for each study and compare with the critical values: $\pm 2.306$
      for 10 pairs and $\pm 1.984$ for 100 pairs.
    options:
      - text: Only the one from the study with 100 pairs
        correct: true
      - text: Only the one from the study with 10 pairs
      - text: Both, because the correlations are the same
      - text: Neither, because .30 is not a strong enough correlation
    hint: >
      The standard error of the correlation has $n - 2$ in its denominator.
      What does a bigger sample do to $t$?
    explanation: >
      With 10 pairs, $t(8) = .30 / \sqrt{(1 - .09)/8} = 0.89$, well short of
      the critical value of $\pm 2.306$. With 100 pairs,
      $t(98) = .30 / \sqrt{(1 - .09)/98} = 3.11$, beyond the critical value of
      about $\pm 1.98$. The correlation is the same size in both studies; what
      changes is how much evidence it rests on.
```
